extracted.intended_audience: educated Victorian public; cultural critics, policymakers, and engaged middle-class readers
extracted.subtask_description: A cultural-philosophical framework for judging public policies and 'practical operations' (e.g., free-trade, social reforms, marriage laws) by whether they conduce to human perfection and general social well-being rather than being pursued mechanically as ends in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test operations by the free play of consciousness (Hellenise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the natural stream of our consciousness flow over proposed operations; if they stand this test, give them support, but not otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called 'Hellenising' — allow disinterested reflection and the spontaneous play of consciousness to examine schemes rather than accepting them from party or scripture. 'In the meanwhile ... keep testing these operations in the simple way we have indicated, by letting the natural stream of our consciousness flow over them freely; and if they stand this test successfully, then let us give them our commendable interest, but not else.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by progress toward human perfection (general perfection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only absolute good is the progress towards perfection — both individual progress and the progress of humanity as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies, practices, and private acts (e.g., having children, possessing luxuries) are good or bad not in themselves but with reference to whether they further the progress towards perfection. Quoted supports: 'The multitude of the wise is the welfare of the world'; Bishop Wilson and the Imitation cited to reinforce the communal character of perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical pursuit of single ends (fetish-worship of objects like free-trade, population, liberty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pursue one object (production, population, liberty) as an end in itself and treat it as an absolute good divorced from the intelligible law of human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold repeatedly warns against worshipping 'fetishes' — e.g., free-trade valued merely for increasing manufactures/population — which leads to a mechanical and harmful policy. Example: untaxing bread used to create more poor men rather than alleviate poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess policies by their effect on the poor and the aggregate of humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether a policy reduces pauperism and misery or merely multiplies industry/wealth while leaving or creating masses of poor people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete social outcomes (e.g., one pauper to nineteen people) as a test; criticism of free-trade: it may create more centres of industry and many more poor people without reducing overall misery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not defer social judgement solely to scripture or authority (critique of Hebraism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious texts and authoritative pronouncements (the Letter of Scripture) are not sufficient for practical questions (e.g., marriage laws); reason and the necessities of human nature must guide judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishop Wilson's maxim cited: 'Christian duties are founded on reason, not on the sovereign authority of God commanding what he pleases.' Applied to marriage and social policy: God's law alone does not settle modern social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate delicacy of perception and sympathetic tact in personal and social relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Human relations (love, marriage) require refined sympathetic perception that cannot be enforced by external mechanical rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Philistine's defect is lack of delicacy; improvement comes from cultivating sympathy and the ability to enter into another's subtle instincts, governing personal action in harmony with finer feelings rather than rigid legal prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require that production and population increases relate to real subsistence and well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating economic growth or population increases, ask whether the produced goods and the expanded population actually improve people's subsistence and happiness, not merely increase counts of manufactures or numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: silk-stockings may become abundant but bread and bacon (true subsistence) may not; production that does not relate to subsistence can leave many worse off despite increased 'manufactures.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat economic axioms as self-acting laws without planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic generalisations (e.g., population spurs production; subsistence expands with civilisation) are not automatic guarantees; they require planning and consideration of actual relations between production and people's needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold criticises Liberal axioms for being applied as if they would 'put themselves into operation without trouble or planning' and stresses the need to consider contingent social realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether institutions can 'carry along' all fellow-men toward perfection (social inclusivity and feasibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether a proposed operation or policy creates masses too degraded or numerous to be taken along in progress toward perfection, thereby making individual perfection impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture requires that progress be general; 'individual perfection is impossible so long as the rest of mankind are not perfected along with us.' If policy produces unmanageable masses of pauperism, it fails this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer disinterested, non-partisan judgement over party-driven advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid partisan blindness; culture's aim is to float stock habits disinterestedly and to follow what consciousness discovers even when it upsets party lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold repeatedly contrasts partisans (Liberals/Conservatives) with those who can afford to be disinterested. The cultural critic must be able to praise what a party forbids and blame what a party defends if disinterested reflection so decides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical operations should be postponed until clarified by culture and reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not join in or lend support to practical operations until one has grown clearer about the nature of real good and formed a mind from which fruitful reforms can spring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold counsels cultivated inaction until a frame of mind is developed: 'we must still decline to lend a hand to their practical operations, until we ... have grown a little clearer about the nature of real good.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal and social prudence about childbearing as a social responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing children into the world when one cannot afford to keep them is irrational and contrary to the divine order; the multiplication of children should be judged by its effect on progress toward perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold explicitly compares having children to owning horses or pictures — all must be judged by whether they hinder one's own or others' progress toward perfection; condemns the idea that 'children are sent' as a blanket divine justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity alone is insufficient; knowledge and prevention of pauperism are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: While compassion and succour are important, preventing the accumulation of pauperism requires knowledge about social causes and remedies, not mere appeals to charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold recounts a good man's emphasis on succour but insists that the knowledge 'how to prevent their accumulating' is necessary to give these children's moral life and growth a chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the 'intelligible law of things' as the standard of national well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies should be related to a coherent understanding of human life and national happiness — the 'intelligible law of things' — rather than to isolated empirical successes or partisan slogans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He suggests 'Hellenising' free-trade by asking how it is related to the intelligible law of human life and national well-being rather than accepting it as an article of faith.
